extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students learning algebraic topology (readers of Evan Chen's Napkin)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and worked examples describing singular cochains, cohomology groups, functoriality, the universal coefficient theorem, Ext computations, de Rham and Poincaré duality, graded/cohomology ring structure and cup/cross products, with examples (spheres, torus, Klein bottle, projective spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of singular cochain complex C•(X; G) and cohomology H^n(X; G)
rubrics_metrics.description: C•(X; G) is defined to be the dual to the singular chain complex C•(X) (apply Hom(−,G)), called the singular cochain complex; its elements are called cochains. The cohomology groups of X are H^n(X; G) := H^n(C•(X); G) = H^n(C•(X; G)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete description: a 0-cochain is a function X → G; a 1-cochain assigns each 1-simplex an element of G. The coboundary operator δ is dual to ∂; e.g. for ϕ ∈ C0, δϕ([v0,v1]) = ϕ([v0]) − ϕ([v1]). Kernels of coboundaries give cocycles, images give coboundaries, and H^n = cocycles/coboundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module structure remark
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a ring (e.g. Z or R), then H^n(X; G) is not only an abelian group but actually a G-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind coefficient rings give extra algebraic structure on cohomology groups; this affects later ring constructions such as cup products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of H^0(X; G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of ker(C0 δ−→ C1) ≅ H^0(X; G) are cochains that are constant on path-connected components. If X has r (finite) path-connected components, H^0(X) ≅ G^⊕r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with infinite components: for cohomology one gets a direct product ∏α Gα rather than a direct sum; this contrasts with C0(X) being formal finite linear sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of notation: implicit dualization of cochain complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: In this chapter cochain complexes A• are implicitly given by applying Hom(−, G) to a chain complex A•; whenever A• is written it denotes such a dualized complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors will treat cochain complexes as dual complexes throughout; keep that implicit dualization in mind when reading formulas and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality of cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Hom(−, G) is a contravariant functor Cmplx^op → CoCmplx; H^n : CoCmplx → Grp; composing yields H^n(−; G) : Cmplx^op → Grp. Theorem: for every n, H^n(−; G) is a contravariant functor from hTop^op to Grp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a map f: X→Y, there is an induced map f^*: H^n(Y;G) → H^n(X;G). Chain homotopies (e.g. via a prism operator) show homotopic maps induce the same map on cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal coefficient theorem (cohomology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A• be a chain complex of free abelian groups and G an abelian group. There is a natural short exact sequence 0 → Ext(H_{n-1}(A•), G) → H^n(A•; G) —h→ Hom(H_n(A•), G) → 0 which is split, so H^n(A•; G) ≅ Ext(H_{n-1}(A•), G) ⊕ Hom(H_n(A•), G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The map h evaluates a cohomology class on homology cycles; the theorem says cohomology is determined by homology plus an Ext 'error term'. In practice for free H_n the Ext vanishes and H^n ≅ Hom(H_n, G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/construction of Ext functor via free resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a free resolution ... → F1 → F0 → H → 0, apply Hom(−, G) to get a cochain complex; define Ext(H,G) := ker(f2^∨)/im(f1^∨). This definition is independent of the chosen free resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute Ext in practice by choosing convenient free resolutions. Intuitively Ext measures 'maps that should be there but aren't'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of Ext (Lemma 75.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Ext(H⊕H', G) = Ext(H, G) ⊕ Ext(H', G). (b) Ext(H, G) = 0 if H is free. (c) Ext(Z/nZ, G) = G/nG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these rules to compute Ext for finitely-generated abelian groups via decomposition into Z and Z/n summands; part (c) follows from the short free resolution 0→Z —×n→ Z → Z/nZ →0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing cohomology via cellular chains (practical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since C•(X) and Cells•(X) are both free and have the same homology, by the universal coefficient theorem their cohomology groups agree. So one may compute H^n(X; G) using the cellular chain complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often far simpler in computations; the UCT guarantees the result depends only on homology (and G) when chains are free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology of spheres (Example 75.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S^m, all Ext terms vanish since homology is free, so H^n(S^m; G) ≅ Hom(H_n(S^m), G) which is G if n=m or n=0, and 0 otherwise (with the coefficient group G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply UCT and known homology of spheres to obtain cohomology groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology of the torus (Example 75.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: H^n(S^1×S^1; G) ≅ Hom(H_n(S^1×S^1), G). Since H_n are Z, Z⊕Z, Z in appropriate dimensions, cohomology groups mirror these as Hom(...,G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again Ext vanishes because homology is free; yields H^0≅G, H^1≅G⊕G, H^2≅G.

rubrics_metrics.name: 0th and 1st cohomology duality (Lemma 75.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n = 0 and n = 1, H^n(X; G) ≅ Hom(H_n(X), G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For n=1 this uses that H0(X) is free so the Ext term in UCT vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Klein bottle cohomology example (with Ext term)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is the Klein bottle with homology H0 = Z, H1 = Z ⊕ Z/2Z, H2 = 0, then H^0(K; G) ≅ G, H^1(K;G) ≅ G ⊕ Hom(Z/2Z, G), and H^2(K;G) ≅ G/2G (coming from Ext(Z/2Z,G) = G/2G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demonstrates a nonzero Ext term contributing to higher cohomology; Hom(Z/2Z,G) is the subgroup of elements of order 2 in G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization of cochains/cocycles/coboundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Cn(X; G) consists of functions assigning each singular n-simplex a value in G (extends linearly). Zn(X; G) = ker δ are cocycles and Bn(X; G) = im δ are coboundaries, so H^n = Zn/Bn. For G a field: cocycles send boundaries to 0; coboundaries send cycles to 0 (one direction always true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cochains need not be alternating or respect reparametrization (unlike differential forms). Homotopic chains with same boundary are mapped to the same value by cocycles. Cocycles modulo coboundaries are essentially determined by their values on cycles modulo boundaries; this is why H^n is closely related to Hom(H_n,G) with Ext the obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative and reduced cohomology definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative cohomology H^n(X,A;G) is defined by dualizing the relative chain complex C•(X,A). Reduced cohomology êH^n(X;G) for nonempty X is defined as H^n(X, {∗};G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can obtain reduced cohomology by augmenting the chain complex with Z and dualizing; UCT still applies because added Z is free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedge-sum cohomology decomposition (Problem 75A⋆ / Theorem 76.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any coefficients G and any n, êH^n(X ∨ Y; G) ≅ êH^n(X; G) ⊕ êH^n(Y; G). More strongly as graded pseudo-rings: êH•(X ∨ Y; R) ≅ êH•(X; R) × êH•(Y; R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The isomorphism comes from restricting cochains on X∨Y to X and Y via the inclusions; product structure respects cup product because cross terms vanish under the wedge decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré duality (Theorem 76.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a smooth oriented compact n-manifold then there is a natural isomorphism H^k(M; Z) ≅ H_{n-k}(M; Z) for every k. In particular H^k(M)=0 for k>n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields Betti number symmetry bk = b_{n-k}. The theorem requires orientation and compactness (and smoothness in this presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: de Rham theorem (Theorem 76.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any smooth manifold M, H^k(M; R) ≅ H^k_{dR}(M), the cohomology of the de Rham complex (closed forms modulo exact forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over R the Ext terms vanish for finitely generated homology groups, so singular cohomology with real coefficients matches de Rham cohomology. Intuition: differential forms can be viewed as cochains satisfying extra smoothness/linearity conditions; the intersections of cocycles/coboundaries with forms give the same quotient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and flavors of graded rings (Definitions 76.3.1–3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A graded pseudo-ring R = ⊕_{d≥0} R_d is an abelian group with an associative multiplication sending R_d × R_e to R_{d+e}. A graded ring additionally has a 1; anticommutative graded rings satisfy rs = (−1)^{|r||s|} sr for homogeneous elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Z[x] as commutative graded ring; exterior algebra ∧^•(V) anticommutative; differential forms Ω•(M) an anticommutative ring under ∧. Note the taxonomy (pseudo-ring vs ring, anticommutative vs commutative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedge product descends to de Rham cohomology (Lemma 76.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wedge product induces ∧ : H^k_{dR}(M) × H^ℓ_{dR}(M) → H^{k+ℓ}_{dR}(M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses d(α∧β) = dα∧β + (−1)^|α| α∧dβ; closed forms wedge to closed forms and wedge with exact gives exact, so product is well-defined on cohomology classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cup product on singular cochains (Definition 76.4.1) and induced cohomology product
rubrics_metrics.description: For ϕ ∈ C^k(X;R), ψ ∈ C^ℓ(X;R), define (ϕ ⌣ ψ)([v0,...,v_{k+ℓ}]) = ϕ([v0,...,v_k]) · ψ([v_k,...,v_{k+ℓ}]). The cup product satisfies δ(ϕ⌣ψ) = δϕ⌣ψ + (−1)^k ϕ⌣δψ, so it induces ⌣ : H^k × H^ℓ → H^{k+ℓ}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cup product makes H•(X;R) into a graded (anti)commutative ring. Warning: cup product on cochains is not literally the wedge product on forms (no alternation), but under de Rham isomorphism the induced ring structures agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticommutativity and cohomology ring structure (Proposition 76.4.5 and Theorem 76.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: H•(X;R) is an anticommutative graded ring: ϕ ⌣ ψ = (−1)^{kℓ} ψ ⌣ ϕ for homogeneous classes. For smooth manifolds, the de Rham isomorphism extends to an isomorphism of anticommutative rings H•(M;R) ≅ H•_{dR}(M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate anticommutativity and situations where anticommutative rings are also commutative (e.g. Z/2Z coefficients or degree parity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of cohomology rings (torus, spheres, projective spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Torus: H•(S^1×S^1;Z) generated by α,β in degree 1 with relations α⌣α=β⌣β=0, α⌣β=−β⌣α, giving Z⊕(αZ⊕βZ)⊕(α⌣β)Z. Sphere S^n: H•(S^n;Z) ≅ Z[α]/(α^2) with |α|=n. RP^n and CP^n: H•(RP^n; Z/2Z) ≅ Z/2Z[α]/(α^{n+1}) with |α|=1, and H•(CP^n; Z) ≅ Z[β]/(β^{n+1}) with |β|=2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples show how cup products detect nontrivial ring structure distinguishing spaces (e.g. CP^2 vs S^2∨S^4). Exercises given to compute cup products explicitly (e.g. α⌣α in RP^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative cup product and reduced cohomology pseudo-rings
rubrics_metrics.description: If A⊆X, there is a relative cup product H^k(X,A;R) × H^ℓ(X,A;R) → H^{k+ℓ}(X,A;R). Define H•(X,A;R) and reduced êH•(X;R); these are anticommutative pseudo-rings (may lack identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functoriality holds: H•(−;R): hTop^op → GradedRings and H•(−,−;R): hPairTop^op → GradedPseudoRings. Cup product of classes vanishes if one factor restricts to zero on A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of graded pseudo-rings (Definition) and wedge sum ring decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The product pseudo-ring R × S is defined degreewise by R_d ⊕ S_d with multiplication coming from R and S and cross products declared zero. Theorem: êH•(X∨Y;R) ≅ êH•(X;R) × êH•(Y;R) as graded pseudo-rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural decomposition explains how wedge sums split cohomology rings and why cup products mixing X and Y vanish. Examples compare CP^2 (generator α with α^2≠0) vs S^2∨S^4 where degree-2 generator squares to 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rough heuristic: if X has an m-dimensional hole and Y has an n-dimensional hole, then X × Y has an (m+n)-dimensional hole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates the cross product construction in (co)homology which will be formalized to connect product spaces' (co)homology to those of the factors (Künneth/Cross product sections follow).
